{{Short description|Type of topological order in condensed matter physics}}
{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}
'''Symmetry-protected topological (SPT) order'''<ref name="defspt">{{cite journal | last1=Gu | first1=Zheng-Cheng | last2=Wen | first2=Xiao-Gang |author-link2=Xiao-Gang Wen| title=Tensor-entanglement-filtering renormalization approach and symmetry-protected topological order | journal=Physical Review B | volume=80 | issue=15 | date=26 October 2009 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.80.155131 | article-number=155131|arxiv=0903.1069 | bibcode=2009PhRvB..80o5131G| s2cid=15114579 }}</ref><ref name="Pollmann Berg Turner Oshikawa p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Pollmann | first1=Frank | last2=Berg | first2=Erez | last3=Turner | first3=Ari M. | last4=Oshikawa | first4=Masaki | title=Symmetry protection of topological phases in one-dimensional quantum spin systems | journal=Physical Review B | volume=85 | issue=7 | date=22 February 2012 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.85.075125 | article-number=075125|arxiv=0909.4059 | bibcode=2012PhRvB..85g5125P| s2cid=53135907 }}</ref> is a kind of order in [[absolute zero|zero-temperature]] quantum-mechanical states of matter that have  a symmetry and a finite energy gap.

To derive the results in a most-invariant way, [[renormalization group|renormalization group methods]] are used (leading to equivalence classes corresponding to certain fixed points).<ref name="defspt" /> The SPT order  has the following defining properties:

(a) ''distinct SPT states with a given symmetry cannot be smoothly deformed into each other without a phase transition, if the deformation preserves the symmetry''. <br />(b) ''however, they all can be smoothly deformed into the same trivial product state without a phase transition, if the symmetry is broken during the deformation''.

The above definition works for both bosonic systems and fermionic systems, which leads to the notions of bosonic SPT order and fermionic SPT order.

Using the notion of [[quantum entanglement]], we can say that SPT states are [[short-range entanglement|short-range entangled]] states ''with a symmetry'' (by contrast: for long-range entanglement see [[topological order]], which is not related to the famous [[EPR paradox]]).  Since short-range entangled states have only trivial [[topological order]]s we may also refer the SPT order as Symmetry Protected "Trivial" order.

==Characteristic properties==

# The boundary effective theory of a non-trivial SPT state always has pure [[Anomaly matching condition|gauge anomaly]] or mixed gauge-gravity anomaly for the symmetry group.<ref name="Wen p. ">{{cite journal | last=Wen | first=Xiao-Gang | title=Classifying gauge anomalies through symmetry-protected trivial orders and classifying gravitational anomalies through topological orders | journal=Physical Review D | volume=88 | issue=4 | date=9 August 2013 | issn=1550-7998 | doi=10.1103/physrevd.88.045013 | article-number=045013|arxiv=1303.1803| bibcode=2013PhRvD..88d5013W | s2cid=18250786 }}</ref> As a result, the boundary of a SPT state is either gapless or degenerate, regardless how we cut the sample to form the boundary. A gapped non-degenerate boundary is impossible for a non-trivial SPT state.  If the boundary is a gapped degenerate state, the degeneracy may be caused by  spontaneous symmetry breaking and/or (intrinsic) topological order.
# [[Monodromy defects]] in non-trivial 2+1D SPT states carry non-trival statistics<ref name="Levin Gu p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Levin | first1=Michael | last2=Gu | first2=Zheng-Cheng | title=Braiding statistics approach to symmetry-protected topological phases | journal=Physical Review B | volume=86 | issue=11 | date=10 September 2012 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.86.115109 | page=114109|arxiv=1202.3120| bibcode=2012PhRvB..86k5109L | s2cid=118688476 }}</ref> and fractional quantum numbers<ref>{{cite journal | last=Wen | first=Xiao-Gang | title=Symmetry-protected topological invariants of symmetry-protected topological phases of interacting bosons and fermions | journal=Physical Review B | volume=89 | issue=3 | date=31 January 2014 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.89.035147 | article-number=035147|arxiv=1301.7675| bibcode=2014PhRvB..89c5147W | s2cid=55842699 }}</ref> of the symmetry group. Monodromy defects are created by twisting the boundary condition along a cut by a symmetry transformation. The ends of such cut are the [[monodromy]] defects. For example, 2+1D bosonic Z<sub>n</sub> SPT states are classified by a Z<sub>n</sub> integer ''m''. One can show that ''n'' identical elementary monodromy defects in a Z<sub>n</sub> SPT state labeled by ''m'' will carry a total Z<sub>n</sub> [[quantum number]] ''2m'' which is not a multiple of ''n''. 
# 2+1D bosonic U(1) SPT states have a Hall conductance that is quantized as an even integer.<ref name="Lu Vishwanath p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Lu | first1=Yuan-Ming | last2=Vishwanath | first2=Ashvin | title=Theory and classification of interacting integer topological phases in two dimensions: A Chern-Simons approach | journal=Physical Review B | volume=86 | issue=12 | date=14 September 2012 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.86.125119 | article-number=125119|arxiv=1205.3156| bibcode=2012PhRvB..86l5119L | s2cid=86856666 }}</ref><ref name="Liu Mei Ye Wen p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Liu | first1=Zheng-Xin | last2=Mei | first2=Jia-Wei | last3=Ye | first3=Peng | last4=Wen | first4=Xiao-Gang | title=U(1)×U(1)symmetry-protected topological order in Gutzwiller wave functions | journal=Physical Review B | volume=90 | issue=23 | date=24 December 2014 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.90.235146 | article-number=235146|arxiv=1408.1676| bibcode=2014PhRvB..90w5146L | s2cid=14800302 }}</ref> 2+1D bosonic SO(3) SPT states have a quantized spin Hall conductance.<ref name="Liu Wen p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Liu | first1=Zheng-Xin | last2=Wen | first2=Xiao-Gang | title=Symmetry-Protected Quantum Spin Hall Phases in Two Dimensions | journal=Physical Review Letters | volume=110 | issue=6 | date=7 February 2013 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.110.067205 | article-number=067205| pmid=23432300 |arxiv=1205.7024| bibcode=2013PhRvL.110f7205L | s2cid=12995741 }}</ref>

==Relation between SPT order and (intrinsic) topological order==
SPT states are short-range entangled while topologically ordered states are long-range entangled.
Both intrinsic [[topological order]], and also SPT order, can sometimes have protected [[gapless boundary excitation]]s. The difference is subtle: the gapless boundary excitations in intrinsic [[topological order]] can be robust against any local perturbations, while the gapless boundary excitations in SPT order are robust only against local perturbations ''that do not break the symmetry''. So the gapless boundary excitations in intrinsic [[topological order]] are topologically protected, while the gapless boundary excitations in SPT order are ''symmetry protected''.<ref>One should also note the semantical subtleness of the name SPT: "symmetry protected"  does not mean that the stability of the state is  conserved "because of the symmetry", but it is  just meant that the symmetry is ''kept'' by the interactions corresponding to the process.</ref>

We also know that an intrinsic [[topological order]] has emergent [[fractional charge]], emergent [[fractional statistics]], and emergent [[gauge theory]]. In contrast, a SPT order has no emergent [[fractional charge]]/[[fractional statistics]] for finite-energy excitations, nor emergent [[gauge theory]] (due to its short-range entanglement). Note that the monodromy defects discussed above are not finite-energy excitations in the spectrum of the Hamiltonian, but defects created by '''modifying''' the Hamiltonian.

==Examples==

The first example of SPT order is the [[AKLT|Haldane phase]] of odd-integer [[spin chain]].<ref name="Haldane pp. 1153–1156">{{cite journal | last=Haldane | first=F. D. M. | title=Nonlinear Field Theory of Large-Spin Heisenberg Antiferromagnets: Semiclassically Quantized Solitons of the One-Dimensional Easy-Axis Néel State | journal=Physical Review Letters | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=50 | issue=15 | date=11 April 1983 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.50.1153 | pages=1153–1156| doi-access=free | bibcode=1983PhRvL..50.1153H }}</ref><ref name="Haldane 1983 pp. 464–468">{{cite journal | last=Haldane | first=F.D.M. | title=Continuum dynamics of the 1-D Heisenberg antiferromagnet: Identification with the O(3) nonlinear sigma model | journal=Physics Letters A | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=93 | issue=9 | year=1983 | issn=0375-9601 | doi=10.1016/0375-9601(83)90631-x | pages=464–468 | bibcode=1983PhLA...93..464H}}</ref><ref name="Affleck Haldane pp. 5291–5300">{{cite journal | last1=Affleck | first1=Ian | last2=Haldane | first2=F. D. M. | title=Critical theory of quantum spin chains | journal=Physical Review B | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=36 | issue=10 | date=1 September 1987 | issn=0163-1829 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.36.5291 | pages=5291–5300 | pmid=9942166 | bibcode=1987PhRvB..36.5291A}}</ref><ref name="Affleck pp. 3047–3072">{{cite journal | last=Affleck | first=I | title=Quantum spin chains and the Haldane gap | journal=Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter | publisher=IOP Publishing | volume=1 | issue=19 | date=15 May 1989 | issn=0953-8984 | doi=10.1088/0953-8984/1/19/001 | pages=3047–3072 | bibcode=1989JPCM....1.3047A| s2cid=250850599 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mishra |first1=Shantanu |last2=Catarina |first2=Gonçalo |last3=Wu |first3=Fupeng |last4=Ortiz |first4=Ricardo |last5=Jacob |first5=David |last6=Eimre |first6=Kristjan |last7=Ma |first7=Ji |last8=Pignedoli |first8=Carlo A. |last9=Feng |first9=Xinliang |last10=Ruffieux |first10=Pascal |last11=Fernández-Rossier |first11=Joaquín |last12=Fasel |first12=Roman |title=Observation of fractional edge excitations in nanographene spin chains |journal=Nature |date=13 October 2021 |volume=598 |issue=7880 |pages=287–292 |doi=10.1038/s41586-021-03842-3|pmid=34645998 |arxiv=2105.09102 |bibcode=2021Natur.598..287M |s2cid=234777902 }}</ref> It is a SPT phase protected by [[SO(3)]] spin rotation symmetry.<ref name=defspt/>  Note that Haldane phases of even-integer-spin chain do not have SPT order.
A more well known example of SPT order is the [[topological insulator]] of non-interacting fermions, a SPT phase protected by [[U(1)]] and [[time reversal symmetry]].

On the other hand, fractional [[quantum Hall effect|quantum Hall]] states are not SPT states. They are states with (intrinsic) topological order and long-range entanglements.

==Group cohomology theory for SPT phases==

Using the notion of [[quantum entanglement]], one obtains the following general picture of gapped
phases at zero temperature. All gapped zero-temperature phases can be divided into two classes: [[long-range entanglement|long-range entangled]] phases (''ie'' phases with intrinsic [[topological order]]) and [[short-range entanglement|short-range entangled]] phases (''ie'' phases with no intrinsic [[topological order]]). All short-range entangled phases can be further divided into three classes:  [[Spontaneous symmetry breaking|symmetry-breaking]] phases, SPT phases, and their mix (symmetry breaking order and SPT order can appear together).

It is well known that [[Spontaneous symmetry breaking|symmetry-breaking]] orders are described by [[group theory]]. For bosonic SPT phases with pure gauge anomalous boundary, it was shown that they are classified by [[group cohomology]] theory:<ref name=spt>{{cite journal | last1=Chen | first1=Xie | last2=Liu | first2=Zheng-Xin | last3=Wen | first3=Xiao-Gang |author-link3=Xiao-Gang Wen|title=Two-dimensional symmetry-protected topological orders and their protected gapless edge excitations | journal=Physical Review B | volume=84 | issue=23 | date=22 December 2011 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.84.235141 | article-number=235141|arxiv=1106.4752 | bibcode=2011PhRvB..84w5141C| s2cid=55330505 }}</ref><ref name="Chen Gu Liu Wen p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Chen | first1=Xie | last2=Gu | first2=Zheng-Cheng | last3=Liu | first3=Zheng-Xin | last4=Wen | first4=Xiao-Gang |author-link4=Xiao-Gang Wen| title=Symmetry protected topological orders and the group cohomology of their symmetry group | journal=Physical Review B | volume=87 | issue=15 | date=4 April 2013 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.87.155114 | article-number=155114|arxiv=1106.4772| bibcode=2013PhRvB..87o5114C | s2cid=118546600 }}</ref> those (d+1)D SPT states with symmetry ''G'' are labeled by the elements in group cohomology class
<math>H^{d+1} [G, U(1)]</math>.
For other (d+1)D SPT states<ref name="Vishwanath Senthil p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Vishwanath | first1=Ashvin | last2=Senthil | first2=T. | title=Physics of Three-Dimensional Bosonic Topological Insulators: Surface-Deconfined Criticality and Quantized Magnetoelectric Effect | journal=Physical Review X | volume=3 | issue=1 | date=28 February 2013 | issn=2160-3308 | doi=10.1103/physrevx.3.011016 | article-number=011016|doi-access=free|arxiv=1209.3058| bibcode=2013PhRvX...3a1016V }}</ref>
<ref> 
 Anton Kapustin, "Symmetry Protected Topological Phases, Anomalies, and Cobordisms: Beyond Group Cohomology" [https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.1467 arXiv:1403.1467]</ref>
<ref name="Wang Gu Wen p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Wang | first1=Juven C. | last2=Gu | first2=Zheng-Cheng | last3=Wen | first3=Xiao-Gang | title=Field-Theory Representation of Gauge-Gravity Symmetry-Protected Topological Invariants, Group Cohomology, and Beyond | journal=Physical Review Letters | volume=114 | issue=3 | date=22 January 2015 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.114.031601 | article-number=031601| pmid=25658993 |arxiv=1405.7689| bibcode=2015PhRvL.114c1601W | s2cid=2370407 }}</ref>
<ref name="Kapustin Thorngren Turzillo Wang 2015 pp. 1–21">{{cite journal | last1=Kapustin | first1=Anton | last2=Thorngren | first2=Ryan | last3=Turzillo | first3=Alex | last4=Wang | first4=Zitao | title=Fermionic symmetry protected topological phases and cobordisms | journal=Journal of High Energy Physics | volume=2015 | issue=12 | year=2015 | issn=1029-8479 | doi=10.1007/jhep12(2015)052 | pages=1–21|arxiv=1406.7329| bibcode=2015JHEP...12..052K | s2cid=42613274 }}</ref> with mixed gauge-gravity anomalous boundary, they can be described by <math>\oplus_{k=1}^d H^k[G,iTO^{d+1-k}]</math>,<ref>{{cite journal | last=Wen | first=Xiao-Gang |author-link=Xiao-Gang Wen| title=Construction of bosonic symmetry-protected-trivial states and their topological invariants via G×SO(∞) nonlinear σ models | journal=Physical Review B | volume=91 | issue=20 | date=4 May 2015 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.91.205101 | article-number=205101|arxiv=1410.8477| bibcode=2015PhRvB..91t5101W | s2cid=13950401 }}</ref> where <math>iTO^{d+1}</math> is the [[Abelian group]] formed by (d+1)D topologically ordered phases that have no non-trivial topological excitations (referred as iTO phases).

From the above results, many new quantum states of matter are predicted, including bosonic topological insulators (the SPT states protected by U(1) and time-reversal symmetry) and bosonic topological superconductors (the SPT states protected by time-reversal symmetry), as well as many other new SPT states protected by other symmetries.

'''A list of bosonic SPT states from group cohomology''' <math>H^{d+1} [G, U(1)]\oplus_{k=1}^d H^k[G,iTO^{d+1-k}]</math> (<math>Z_2^T</math> = time-reversal-symmetry group)
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! symmetry group !! 1+1D !! 2+1D !! 3+1D !! 4+1D !! comment
|-
| <math>0</math> || <math>0</math> || <math>Z</math> || <math>0</math> || <math>Z_2</math> ||iTO phases with no symmetry: <math>iTO^{d+1}</math>
|-
| <math>U(1) \rtimes Z_2^T</math> || <math>Z_2</math> || <math>Z_2</math> || <math>2Z_2+Z_2</math> || <math>Z\oplus Z_2+Z</math> || bosonic topological insulator
|-
| <math>Z_2^T</math> || <math>Z_2</math> || <math>0</math> || <math>Z_2+Z_2</math> || <math>0</math> || bosonic topological superconductor
|-
| <math>Z_n</math> || <math>0</math> || <math>Z_n</math> || <math>0</math> ||  <math>Z_n+Z_n</math> ||
|-
| <math>U(1)</math> || <math>0</math> || <math>Z</math> || <math>0</math> || <math>Z+Z</math> ||2+1D: quantum Hall effect
|-
| <math>SO(3)</math> || <math>Z_2</math> || <math>Z</math> || <math>0</math> ||<math>Z_2</math> || 1+1D: odd-integer-spin chain; 2+1D: spin Hall effect
|-
| <math>SO(3)\times Z_2^T</math> || <math>2Z_2</math> || <math>Z_2</math> || <math>3Z_2+Z_2</math> || <math>2Z_2</math> ||
|-
| <math>Z_2\times Z_2\times Z_2^T</math> || <math>4Z_2</math> || <math>6Z_2</math> || <math>9Z_2+Z_2</math> || <math>12Z_2+2Z_2</math> ||
|}
The phases before "+" come from <math>H^{d+1} [G, U(1)]</math>. The phases after "+" come from <math>\oplus_{k=1}^d H^k[G,iTO^{d+1-k}]</math>.
Just like group theory can give us 230 crystal structures in 3+1D, [[group cohomology]] theory can give us various SPT phases in any dimensions with any on-site symmetry groups.

On the other hand, the fermionic SPT orders are described by [[group super-cohomology]] theory.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Gu | first1=Zheng-Cheng | last2=Wen | first2=Xiao-Gang |author-link2=Xiao-Gang Wen| title=Symmetry-protected topological orders for interacting fermions: Fermionic topological nonlinear σ models and a special group supercohomology theory | journal=Physical Review B | volume=90 | issue=11 | date=23 September 2014 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.90.115141 | article-number=115141|arxiv=1201.2648| bibcode=2014PhRvB..90k5141G | s2cid=119307777 }}</ref> So the group (super-)cohomology theory allows us to construct many
SPT orders even for interacting systems, which include  interacting topological insulator/superconductor.

==A complete classification of 1D gapped quantum phases (with interactions)==

Using the notions of [[quantum entanglement]] and SPT order, one can obtain
a complete classification of all 1D gapped [[quantum phases]].

First, it is shown that there is no (intrinsic) [[topological order]] in 1D (''i.e.'', all 1D gapped states
are short-range entangled).<ref name="Verstraete Cirac Latorre Rico p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Verstraete | first1=F. | last2=Cirac | first2=J. I. | last3=Latorre | first3=J. I. | last4=Rico | first4=E. | last5=Wolf | first5=M. M. | title=Renormalization-Group Transformations on Quantum States | journal=Physical Review Letters | volume=94 | issue=14 | date=14 April 2005 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.94.140601 | article-number=140601| pmid=15904055 | arxiv=quant-ph/0410227 | bibcode=2005PhRvL..94n0601V | s2cid=21362387 }}</ref>
Thus, if the Hamiltonians have no symmetry, all their 1D gapped quantum states belong to one phase—the phase of trivial product states.
On the other hand, if the Hamiltonians do have a symmetry,  their 1D gapped quantum states 
are either [[Spontaneous symmetry breaking|symmetry-breaking]] phases, SPT phases, or their mix.

Such an understanding allows one to classify all 1D gapped quantum phases:<ref name=spt/><ref name="Chen Gu Wen p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Chen | first1=Xie | last2=Gu | first2=Zheng-Cheng | last3=Wen | first3=Xiao-Gang | title=Classification of gapped symmetric phases in one-dimensional spin systems | journal=Physical Review B | volume=83 | issue=3 | date=13 January 2011 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.83.035107 | article-number=035107|arxiv=1008.3745 | bibcode=2011PhRvB..83c5107C| s2cid=9139955 }}</ref><ref name="Turner Pollmann Berg p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Turner | first1=Ari M. | last2=Pollmann | first2=Frank | last3=Berg | first3=Erez | title=Topological phases of one-dimensional fermions: An entanglement point of view | journal=Physical Review B | volume=83 | issue=7 | date=8 February 2011 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.83.075102 | article-number=075102|arxiv=1008.4346| bibcode=2011PhRvB..83g5102T | s2cid=118491997 }}</ref><ref name="Fidkowski Kitaev p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Fidkowski | first1=Lukasz | last2=Kitaev | first2=Alexei |author-link2=Alexei Kitaev | title=Topological phases of fermions in one dimension | journal=Physical Review B | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=83 | issue=7 | date=8 February 2011 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.83.075103 | article-number=075103|arxiv=1008.4138| bibcode=2011PhRvB..83g5103F | s2cid=1201670 }}</ref><ref name="Schuch Pérez-García Cirac p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Schuch | first1=Norbert | last2=Pérez-García | first2=David | last3=Cirac | first3=Ignacio | title=Classifying quantum phases using matrix product states and projected entangled pair states | journal=Physical Review B | volume=84 | issue=16 | date=31 October 2011 | issn=1098-0121 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.84.165139 | article-number=165139|arxiv=1010.3732| bibcode=2011PhRvB..84p5139S | s2cid=74872240 }}</ref> All 1D gapped phases are classified by
the following three mathematical objects: <math>(G_H, G_\Psi, H^{2} [G_\Psi , U(1)])</math> , where <math>G_H</math> is the symmetry group of the Hamiltonian, <math>G_\Psi</math> the symmetry group of the ground states, and <math>H^{2} [G_\Psi, U(1)]</math> the second [[group cohomology]] class of <math>G_\Psi</math>. (Note that <math>H^{2} [G, U(1)]</math> classifies the projective representations of <math>G</math>.) If there is no symmetry breaking (''ie'' <math>G_\Psi=G_H</math>), the 1D gapped phases are classified by the projective representations of symmetry group <math>G_H</math>.
